outcome: Still open in general. The one in-window result on the bullet is Cheng and Sgueglia's preprint of 10 July 2026, which proves only an asymptotic version (for large even n, K_n has a 1-factorisation in which (1−ε)n of the 1-factors are pairwise perfect), not a perfect 1-factorisation of any K_n, and whose central construction its authors credit to ChatGPT 5.4. No perfect 1-factorisation of a new order was found in the window; the sources report K_64 as the smallest even order with none known.
problem_asks: (i) For every even order N (sources differ on whether the range starts at N = 2 or N = 4; K_2 is trivial): the complete graph K_N has a 1-factorisation, that is, its edge set splits into N−1 pairwise disjoint perfect matchings (1-factors). (ii) That 1-factorisation is perfect: the union of ANY two of its 1-factors is a single Hamiltonian cycle, so all C(N−1, 2) pairs of 1-factors must satisfy this, not most of them. (iii) The claim is universal in N: no lower bound on N, no exceptional orders, asked for every even N and not for one order or for large N only.

events.what_happened: Anton Kotzig stated the conjecture at the first international graph-theory conference at Smolenice (June 1963; the write-up is in the 1964 proceedings Theory of Graphs and its Applications, Prague) and observed that a folklore 1-factorisation of K_n is perfect whenever n−1 is prime: the vertices are the corners of a regular (n−1)-gon plus one centre vertex, and the 1-factors are rotations of a matching of edges perpendicular to a fixed direction. Both the Cheng–Sgueglia introduction and the Pike introduction (both opened, HTML) attribute the conjecture to Kotzig in 1963 with the 1964 reference, and the n−1 prime case to Kotzig. I did not open the 1964 proceedings.
events.delivers: A perfect 1-factorisation of K_n for every even n with n−1 prime (orders p+1, p prime). This is an infinite family of orders, not all even orders.
events.remains: Every even order n with n−1 composite, and the statement as a whole.
events.time_since_posted: about 62 years from the 1964 proceedings; every later source I opened treats the conjecture as open.
events.directly_checkable: The construction is explicit. For a given n with n−1 prime, the pairwise Hamiltonicity of the rotational 1-factors can be checked by hand or by machine. Pike's introduction says testing any given 1-factorisation for perfectness is straightforward.
events.doubts: One search snippet says Kotzig showed K_2m is perfect 'if and only if' 2m−1 is prime. The sources I opened state only the 'if' direction (the folklore construction is perfect when n−1 is prime). The 'only if' claim is unverified and I did not record it as established.
events.direction: Supports the conjecture on an infinite family of orders. No counterexample involved.
events.object: An explicit 1-factorisation of K_n for n−1 prime: the rotations of one perpendicular-edge matching in a regular (n−1)-gon with a centre vertex. Explicit for each n; its perfectness follows from the primality of n−1 by the rotation argument that Kotzig gave.

events.what_happened: Stefan Glock and Amedeo Sgueglia, 'On Kotzig's conjecture in random graphs', arXiv:2510.01949, v1 submitted 2 Oct 2025, v2 revised 25 Sep 2026 (current; the comments field says 'final version as accepted for publication in Journal of Combinatorial Theory, Series B'). Studies a random-graph variant: for each fixed k there is C = C(k) such that for p ≥ C log n / n, G(n,p) contains with high probability k edge-disjoint perfect matchings, every pair of which forms a Hamilton cycle. The main tool is a counting theorem for K_n: for any k edge-disjoint perfect matchings of K_n, a uniformly random perfect matching forms a Hamilton cycle with each of them with probability Θ_k(n^{−k/2}).

events.what_happened: Yangyang Cheng and Amedeo Sgueglia, 'The perfect 1-factorisation conjecture holds asymptotically', arXiv:2607.09459 (math.CO; 6 pages, 2 figures; one version, v1, submitted 10 Jul 2026, abstract and HTML opened). Abstract: for every even n, K_n can be decomposed into n−1 perfect matchings such that (1−o(1))n of them have the property that any pair forms a Hamilton cycle; the authors say the conjecture is 'far from being solved'. Theorem 1.2 (HTML, read via fetch summary): for every ε > 0 there is n0 such that for every even n ≥ n0, K_n has a 1-factorisation containing (1−ε)n perfect matchings, any two of which form a perfect pair. Theorem 1.3: K_n contains (1−ε)n edge-disjoint perfect matchings, any two forming a perfect pair; the construction rotates a matching around r central vertices, where n−r is an odd prime in [n − n^0.525, n] (prime from Baker–Harman–Pintz). Theorem 1.2 is then obtained by randomly deleting matchings, using Alon–Pokrovskiy–Sudakov, a robust-expander argument, and a Kühn–Osthus Hamilton decomposition of the expander.
events.revisions: v1 only, submitted 10 Jul 2026 (metadata date 13 Jul 2026).
events.delivers: For large even n (n ≥ n0(ε), n0 not made explicit): a 1-factorisation of K_n in which (1−ε)n of the 1-factors are pairwise perfect. The remaining εn 1-factors are unconstrained by the result, and not all pairs of 1-factors are asserted perfect. It gives no perfect 1-factorisation of any K_n, and nothing for small n.
events.remains: Every even n below n0(ε), including the orders reported as open (K_64 per the paper's introduction); the εn exceptional 1-factors in each factorisation; the requirement that every pair of 1-factors be perfect, for every even n.
events.directly_checkable: The Theorem 1.3 matchings are explicit (rotations around r central vertices with n−r an odd prime), so a reader can test pairwise Hamiltonicity for any given even n. I did not run such a check. The Theorem 1.2 factorisation is probabilistic, and no explicit instance is given.
events.doubts: (a) One version; no referee, journal acceptance or public verification found in the searches. (b) The construction that Theorem 1.3, and hence Theorem 1.2, rests on is credited in the paper to ChatGPT 5.4, which the authors say gave 'a correct but rather long proof'; they then present their own shorter proof. Neither has been independently checked. (c) The paper says 'The proof of Theorem 1.2 was entirely obtained by the authors' in the same introduction that credits the Theorem 1.3 construction to the model, and Theorem 1.2 is built on Theorem 1.3. A reader has to decide how these fit. (d) The introduction states, without citation, that 'the current smallest open case is n=64'. (e) The introduction is read here via a summarising fetch tool, so the wording of point (b) should be checked against the raw HTML. No specific error in a key step has been identified by anyone.
events.direction: Cuts in favour of the conjecture, asymptotically: a near-perfect 1-factorisation for large n. No counterexample. Does not decide the bullet as worded.
events.object: Theorem 1.3's construction: for large even n, (1−ε)n edge-disjoint perfect matchings of K_n, pairwise forming Hamilton cycles, built by rotating a matching around r central vertices where n−r is an odd prime (the prime from Baker–Harman–Pintz in [n − n^0.525, n]). Explicit given the prime; the authors describe it as a constructive proof. Theorem 1.2's 1-factorisation extends these matchings probabilistically and is non-constructive. Neither object contradicts the conjecture; neither is a perfect 1-factorisation.

Theorem 1.3's construction is the input to Theorem 1.2, which gives the headline asymptotic result.

disputes.summary: The AI credit in Cheng & Sgueglia (2026) is split. The authors credit ChatGPT 5.4 with the Theorem 1.3 construction and a long proof of it, but say their own proof is 'cleaner, shorter and substantially different' and that Theorem 1.2's proof was 'entirely obtained by the authors'. Theorem 1.2 uses Theorem 1.3's matchings. Recorded as stated; the weighing is for the later pass.

The claim that K_64 is the smallest open even order originates in Pike (2018/2019) and is repeated by Glock & Sgueglia (2025 intro) and Cheng & Sgueglia (2026 intro). The later two are not independent confirmations. Two search summaries (one from an AI-generated review site, not opened) also state n=64 and are not used as sources.

Dates: Kotzig's conjecture is dated 1963 (conference) and 1964 (proceedings) by different sources; Anderson's family is dated 1973 in the Cheng–Sgueglia reference list and 1974 in other snippets. Recorded as the years given, with the disagreement stated in each event.

The number of non-isomorphic perfect 1-factorisations of K_16 is 3155 in both Gill & Wanless (2019/2020) and a search snippet on Meszka's independent computation. The count with a nontrivial automorphism group is 89 (Gill & Wanless), corrected from 88 (Meszka & Rosa, 2003, snippet only).

The Wikipedia article 'Kotzig's conjecture' is a different problem: it concerns P_k-graphs (every pair of vertices joined by exactly one path of length k), not perfect 1-factorisations. It is not an event for this bullet and should not be read as its status.

summary: The bullet is open. I ran 33 WebSearch queries and opened the arXiv abstract pages of the main papers, the HTML versions of the Cheng–Sgueglia (2026), Pike (2018) and Glock–Sgueglia (2025) papers, the Gill–Wanless (2019) and Allsop–Wanless (2025) abstracts, the Lambard (2026, hypercube) abstract, two Monash Wanless pages (the P1F data page and the Bryant–Maenhaut–Wanless abstract), the Wikipedia 'Kotzig's conjecture' page, and two Semantic Scholar citation lists. The PDFs of the three main papers were not decodable, so their body text comes from WebFetch summaries of the HTML versions; quotes are as those summaries returned them, and the AI sentence was returned identically by two separate fetches of the same HTML page. The only in-window result on the statement is Cheng & Sgueglia (arXiv 2607.09459, 10 July 2026). It proves an asymptotic relaxation: for large even n, K_n has a 1-factorisation in which (1−ε)n of the 1-factors are pairwise perfect. It does not establish a perfect 1-factorisation of any K_n, and the authors say the conjecture is 'far from being solved'. Whether that counts as progress on this bullet is a close call that I have left to the later pass: the statement is universal in n with every pair required, and the result is asymptotic with a fraction of exceptional factors. The AI question is also a close call. The paper's 'Comment on the use of AI' says the Theorem 1.3 construction 'was generated by ChatGPT 5.4, which also gave a correct but rather long proof', that the paper's own proof is 'cleaner, shorter and substantially different' and 'obtained by the authors', and that Theorem 1.2's proof was 'entirely obtained by the authors'. Theorem 1.2 is built from the Theorem 1.3 matchings, so the credited construction is load-bearing for the headline; but the authors also call it a generalisation of an opening example, so the model's role could be read as generalising a human construction. I found no other AI involvement in this problem; the searches for AI results on the problem (AlphaEvolve, GPT-5, Gemini, Erdős problems, Lean formalisations, Quanta and Tao coverage) returned nothing relevant. Pre-window events are recorded because they bear on which orders are settled: Kotzig 1964 (n−1 prime), Anderson 1973 (n/2 prime), Dinitz & Stinson 1989 (seven orders, snippet only), Bryant, Maenhaut & Wanless (second factorisation of K_{p+1}), Wanless's 2007 table, Wolfe 2009 (K_52), Pike 2018/2019 (K_56), and Gill & Wanless 2019 (K_16 enumeration). Two in-window results are neighbouring questions and recorded as such: Glock & Sgueglia (random graphs; JCTB accepted) and Allsop & Wanless (bipartite K_{11,11}). The Wikipedia 'Kotzig's conjecture' page is a namesake about P_k-graphs. The Monash data page is stale (last dated entries 2007), so it cannot reflect Wolfe or Pike and its silence about an order is not evidence. The reported smallest open order, K_64, rests on Pike's 2019 statement; no in-window source found a construction for it.
competing_reading: Read as progress: the Cheng–Sgueglia abstract says 'the conjecture holds asymptotically', and a judge could treat a 1-factorisation of K_n with (1−o(1))n pairwise-perfect factors for all large even n as a partial resolution of the 'for every even n' claim in the limit. Read against that: the bullet asks for every pair of 1-factors in every even order, and the result gives neither the exact range nor the full pair requirement. Read as AI-incidental: the authors call Theorem 1.3's construction a generalisation of an opening example, say the paper's own proof is 'substantially different', and say Theorem 1.2's proof was 'entirely obtained by the authors'; on that reading the model supplied a step the humans then re-proved, not the mathematics the result rests on. Read against that: Theorem 1.2 is built directly on the Theorem 1.3 matchings, so the construction is load-bearing whichever proof is used.
what_would_settle_it: The raw LaTeX or HTML source of arXiv 2607.09459, to confirm the 'Comment on the use of AI' paragraph and the Theorem 1.2 proof sentence word for word (both are currently read through a fetch summary). Any later version, journal submission or referee report for 2607.09459. An independent check that the Theorem 1.3 matchings are pairwise perfect for small even n, and an independent review of the proof of Theorem 1.2. The authors' own statement of what ChatGPT 5.4 and the human authors each contributed to Theorem 1.3. For the bullet itself, an explicit perfect 1-factorisation of K_64 or any other order reported as open, or a published reference that changes the 'smallest open order' statement.

event.what_happened: Yangyang Cheng and Amedeo Sgueglia, 'The perfect 1-factorisation conjecture holds asymptotically', arXiv:2607.09459 (math.CO; 6 pages, 2 figures; one version, v1, submitted 10 Jul 2026, abstract and HTML opened). Abstract: for every even n, K_n can be decomposed into n−1 perfect matchings such that (1−o(1))n of them have the property that any pair forms a Hamilton cycle; the authors say the conjecture is 'far from being solved'. Theorem 1.2 (HTML, read via fetch summary): for every ε > 0 there is n0 such that for every even n ≥ n0, K_n has a 1-factorisation containing (1−ε)n perfect matchings, any two of which form a perfect pair. Theorem 1.3: K_n contains (1−ε)n edge-disjoint perfect matchings, any two forming a perfect pair; the construction rotates a matching around r central vertices, where n−r is an odd prime in [n − n^0.525, n] (prime from Baker–Harman–Pintz). Theorem 1.2 is then obtained by randomly deleting matchings, using Alon–Pokrovskiy–Sudakov, a robust-expander argument, and a Kühn–Osthus Hamilton decomposition of the expander.
event.revisions: v1 only, submitted 10 Jul 2026 (metadata date 13 Jul 2026).
event.delivers: For large even n (n ≥ n0(ε), n0 not made explicit): a 1-factorisation of K_n in which (1−ε)n of the 1-factors are pairwise perfect. The remaining εn 1-factors are unconstrained by the result, and not all pairs of 1-factors are asserted perfect. It gives no perfect 1-factorisation of any K_n, and nothing for small n.
event.remains: Every even n below n0(ε), including the orders reported as open (K_64 per the paper's introduction); the εn exceptional 1-factors in each factorisation; the requirement that every pair of 1-factors be perfect, for every even n.
event.directly_checkable: The Theorem 1.3 matchings are explicit (rotations around r central vertices with n−r an odd prime), so a reader can test pairwise Hamiltonicity for any given even n. I did not run such a check. The Theorem 1.2 factorisation is probabilistic, and no explicit instance is given.
event.doubts: (a) One version; no referee, journal acceptance or public verification found in the searches. (b) The construction that Theorem 1.3, and hence Theorem 1.2, rests on is credited in the paper to ChatGPT 5.4, which the authors say gave 'a correct but rather long proof'; they then present their own shorter proof. Neither has been independently checked. (c) The paper says 'The proof of Theorem 1.2 was entirely obtained by the authors' in the same introduction that credits the Theorem 1.3 construction to the model, and Theorem 1.2 is built on Theorem 1.3. A reader has to decide how these fit. (d) The introduction states, without citation, that 'the current smallest open case is n=64'. (e) The introduction is read here via a summarising fetch tool, so the wording of point (b) should be checked against the raw HTML. No specific error in a key step has been identified by anyone.
event.direction: Cuts in favour of the conjecture, asymptotically: a near-perfect 1-factorisation for large n. No counterexample. Does not decide the bullet as worded.
event.object: Theorem 1.3's construction: for large even n, (1−ε)n edge-disjoint perfect matchings of K_n, pairwise forming Hamilton cycles, built by rotating a matching around r central vertices where n−r is an odd prime (the prime from Baker–Harman–Pintz in [n − n^0.525, n]). Explicit given the prime; the authors describe it as a constructive proof. Theorem 1.2's 1-factorisation extends these matchings probabilistically and is non-constructive. Neither object contradicts the conjecture; neither is a perfect 1-factorisation.

judgement.why: The statement is universal over even orders and demands every pair of 1-factors be Hamiltonian. Kotzig (n−1 prime) and Anderson (n/2 prime) settle infinite families of orders, so they are cases; isolated orders (Dinitz–Stinson, Wolfe K_52, Pike K_56) and the K_16 enumeration are finitely many instances of the universal statement; a second factorisation at already-covered orders and the stale data table settle nothing new. Glock–Sgueglia (random graphs, k matchings) and Allsop–Wanless (bipartite K_{11,11}) answer changed questions. The close call is Cheng–Sgueglia: it does not settle any order, but it raises the proportion of pairwise-perfect 1-factors achievable in a 1-factorisation of K_n to 1−o(1) for all large even n. I read that as moving a proportion on a still-open question (bound) rather than as a variant, since the quantity it moves is the one the conjecture wants to equal all n−1 factors. On AI, the authors say ChatGPT 5.4 generated the Theorem 1.3 construction, which Theorem 1.2 is built on. That construction is mathematics in the result, even though the humans re-proved it and wrote the Theorem 1.2 argument themselves, so the event is assisted, not generated.
judgement.doubts: Bound versus variant for Cheng–Sgueglia is arguable: it could be read as a weaker form of the conjecture, and on that reading it would be discarded. The AI quote comes through a fetch summary, not raw source text. Dinitz–Stinson's list of orders rests on OCR'd snippets. Pre-snapshot verification calls rely on journal publication cited from snippets.
